questionText: The manuscript is ____ genuine; what remains at issue is the century in which it was copied.
explanation: Negative 'in-' plus stem plus '-able' plus '-ly', with the silent 'e' dropped. Spanish 'indiscutiblemente' rests on a different root ('discutir'), so learners produce *indiscussably; note that this stem takes 'in-', not 'un-'.

questionText: She retired as the ____ authority on the coinage of the early Islamic world.
explanation: Here the negative prefix is 'un-' plus the past participle, not 'in-': the two prefixes select different suffixes on the same stem, so 'undisputed' and 'indisputable' both exist while *indisputed and *undisputable do not. The attributive slot before 'authority' requires the participle.

questionText: The figures themselves are sound, but the inference drawn from them is highly ____.
explanation: The unnegated '-able' adjective, meaning 'open to challenge'; the contrastive 'but' forbids a negative prefix here. Spanish 'discutible' again supplies the sense without the form, and 'questionable' is the synonym learners default to.

questionText: The contract exempts either party from liability for delays arising from wholly ____ events.
explanation: Negative 'un-' plus stem plus '-able': the event could not have been predicted even in principle. Spanish 'imprevisible' uses a Latin root with no 'see' element, so learners reach for 'unpredictable'; only the '-able' form expresses impossibility rather than mere fact.

questionText: An entirely ____ consequence of the reform was a sharp fall in the number of applications.
explanation: Negative 'un-' plus the irregular past participle 'seen', with no suffix at all. The contrast with the previous form matters: 'unforeseen' states that nobody did predict it, while 'unforeseeable' claims nobody could have.

questionText: It took considerable ____ to acquire the site years before the rail link was even announced.
explanation: Stem mutation 'see' > 'sight' forms an uncountable noun; there is no suffix, which is why the form resists analogy. Spanish 'previsión' tempts *forevision or 'prevision', and the uncountable 'considerable foresight' cannot take an article.

questionText: By the third year of the crisis the province had become effectively ____.
explanation: Negative 'un-' plus stem plus '-able', a double modification. Spanish 'ingobernable' takes 'in-', which is the source of the frequent *ingovernable; English reserves 'in-' for Latinate stems and this one has been fully naturalised.

questionText: The report criticises the charity's ____ rather than the conduct of any individual trustee.
explanation: Nominalising '-ance' denoting the manner in which an institution is run, distinct from 'government', which names the body itself. Spanish and Catalan both use 'gobierno'/'govern' for both senses, so the distinction has to be learned rather than transferred.

questionText: Decades of ____ had hollowed out the very institutions the incoming administration inherited.
explanation: Privative 'mis-' plus stem plus '-ment', a double modification meaning rule that is incompetent rather than merely bad. Spanish 'desgobierno' uses 'des-', prompting *disgovernment; English selects 'mis-' for the sense 'wrongly done'.

questionText: Rising salinity has rendered great swathes of the delta effectively ____.
explanation: Three affixes: 'in-' (here the locative 'in', meaning 'to dwell in') plus '-able', then negated by 'un-'. This is the classic trap of the pair, since 'inhabitable' means fit to live in, not unfit; Spanish 'inhabitable' means the opposite of its English lookalike, making it a genuine false friend.

questionText: He ____ understates his own contribution, which makes the citation record misleading.
explanation: Adjectival '-ual' plus adverbial '-ly' on the bare noun. Spanish 'habitualmente' is a true friend in meaning, but learners frequently write *habitualy with a single 'l', since the Spanish adverb has only one.

questionText: ____ to background noise occurs within minutes, which is why the effect is so hard to measure.
explanation: Verbalising '-uate' plus nominalising '-ion', a double transformation yielding a technical uncountable noun. The competing 'habit' would be ungrammatical as the subject of 'occurs within minutes', and Spanish 'habituación' hides the fact that English also has 'habitation', a wholly unrelated word meaning dwelling.

questionText: The scale of the loss was ____ to anyone who had not seen the valley before the flood.
explanation: Negative 'un-' plus stem plus '-able', silent 'e' dropped. The family's three adjectives are the real test: 'unimaginable' (impossible to conceive), 'unimaginative' (lacking creativity) and 'imaginary' (not real) are distinguished only by suffix.

questionText: The proposal is competent but ____, recycling solutions abandoned a decade ago.
explanation: Negative 'un-' plus '-ative', describing a lack of invention rather than an impossibility. The concessive 'but' after 'competent' fixes the sense: 'unimaginable' would be nonsensical of a proposal that plainly exists.

questionText: The boundary is entirely ____, yet it determines which court has jurisdiction over the wreck.
explanation: Suffix '-ary' meaning 'existing only in the mind'. Spanish 'imaginario' is a true friend, but 'imaginativo' and 'imaginario' are as easily confused in the L1 as their English counterparts; the contrastive 'yet' requires 'not physically real', not 'creative'.

questionText: The building's ____ facade conceals one of the finest private collections in Europe.
explanation: Negative 'un-' plus '-ive', a double modification demanded by the contrast with 'conceals one of the finest'. Spanish 'impresionante' carries a much stronger charge than English 'impressive', so learners over-read the positive form and miss the need for negation.

questionText: Advertising aimed at ____ audiences is subject to considerably stricter regulation.
explanation: Nominalising '-ion' plus '-able', a double transformation meaning 'easily influenced', which is applied to people and not to things. Spanish 'impresionable' exists but is far rarer than 'influenciable', so the form is under-produced.

questionText: The team performed ____ given the constraints of time and budget under which they were working.
explanation: Suffix '-ive' plus adverbial '-ly' modifying the verb 'performed'. Learners regularly supply the adjective here under the influence of Spanish, where 'de forma impresionante' is a prepositional phrase rather than a single adverb.

questionText: The recording is largely ____, so the published transcript rests on a degree of guesswork.
explanation: Negative 'un-' plus the stem branch 'intellig-' plus '-ible', meaning 'impossible to make out'. The whole point of the item is that 'intelligible' has nothing to do with 'intelligent': Spanish 'ininteligible' also takes 'in-', which prompts the frequent *inintelligible.

questionText: The ____ of the signal degrades sharply at distances beyond fifty metres.
explanation: Stem plus '-ible' plus '-ity', with 'ible' > 'ibil' before the suffix. Spanish 'inteligibilidad' is a true friend but is rarely met, and the competing 'intelligence' would make the sentence claim that a signal thinks.

questionText: The report drew almost exclusively on ____ gathered from publicly available sources.
explanation: Suffix '-ence' on the 'intellig-' stem, here in the specialised uncountable sense of gathered information rather than mental capacity. Spanish 'inteligencia' covers both senses too, but learners hesitate to use the English noun without an article, which this uncountable reading requires.

questionText: A ____ plaque was unveiled on the centenary of the disaster in the presence of survivors' families.
explanation: Prefix 'com-' plus the stem with 'y' > 'or' plus verbal '-ate' plus '-ive', the most heavily affixed member of the family. Spanish 'conmemorativo' has an 'n' where English has an 'm', which produces the standard misspelling *conmemorative.

questionText: The film is technically accomplished but ultimately ____; nothing whatever lingers afterwards.
explanation: Negative 'un-' plus stem plus '-able', with 'y' > 'or' before the suffix. Spanish 'memorable' exists, but its negative is normally paraphrased as 'poco memorable', so the single-word negation is under-produced by L1 speakers.

questionText: The passage was ____ described by one early critic as prose set to music.
explanation: Stem plus '-able' plus '-ly', with the '-le' collapsing to '-ly' rather than doubling. The adverbial slot before the past participle 'described' rules out the adjective, and the '-ably' ending is what learners most often get wrong.

questionText: Prolonged ____ following major surgery carries risks of its own, notably thrombosis.
explanation: Negative 'in-' assimilated to 'im-' before the bilabial 'm', plus '-ity'. Spanish 'inmovilidad' keeps the unassimilated 'n', which is why *inmobility is such a persistent error in Spanish and Catalan scripts.

questionText: The ____ of several thousand volunteers within hours of the announcement astonished the organisers.
explanation: Verbalising '-ise/-ize' plus '-ation', with the final 'e' of the base dropped. Both spellings are standard and either is credited; Spanish 'movilización' has a 'v', a frequent source of *mobilización-style hybrids.

questionText: The fracture left him ____ for the better part of an academic term.
explanation: Assimilated 'im-' plus '-ise/-ize' plus participial '-ed', a triple modification. The resultative structure 'left him ____' requires a participle, so the noun 'immobility' cannot fill the gap.

questionText: The chronicler attributes the outbreak to ____ agency rather than to any form of contagion.
explanation: Prefix 'super-' plus stem plus adjectival '-al', with the final 'e' dropped. Spanish 'sobrenatural' uses 'sobre-', so learners occasionally calque it as *overnatural; the contrast with 'contagion' fixes the sense as 'beyond the natural order'.

questionText: The room was ____ quiet, as though the entire building had been evacuated overnight.
explanation: Negative 'un-' plus '-al' plus '-ly', giving the doubled 'n' at the prefix boundary that learners routinely reduce to one. Spanish 'antinatural' and 'poco natural' offer no model for the double consonant.

questionText: ____ requires five years' continuous residence and a recognised language qualification.
explanation: Adjectival '-al' plus verbalising '-ise/-ize' plus '-ation', a triple transformation with a specialised legal sense of acquiring citizenship. Spanish 'nacionalización' is used for this in some varieties, which pushes learners towards the wrong root altogether.
